Testing rvtk with downstream packages

Source: vignettes/rvtk-integration.qmd 
library(rvtk)

Scope and audience

The rvtk vignette is written for downstream package authors: it explains how to link an R package against VTK through rvtk. This vignette is written for rvtk maintainers (and for curious downstream authors who want to know what the CI badge really checks). It describes how rvtk tests itself against other packages that consume it, and how the pre-built VTK archives are validated before they are published.

The guarantees on offer are deliberately layered:

  1. A minimal, scaffolded consumer (downstream-check.yaml) proves that the two setup strategies produce identical build configuration, on every supported platform and VTK strategy.
  2. A real-world consumer (riot-check.yaml) proves that an actual package (riot, the original motivation for rvtk) installs, links, and round-trips its real VTK files.
  3. CRAN-checker environments (prebuilt-audit.yaml) replicate the exact containers CRAN uses for Linux aarch64 and musl, where hosted GitHub runners cannot exercise the archives.
  4. Archive-level gates inside build-vtk-libs.yml run before any archive is packaged: a whole-archive link, a macOS deployment-target check, and a libc++-ABI check.

The minimal consumer: downstream-check.yaml

File: .github/workflows/downstream-check.yaml (604 lines; workflow-level cache-version: downstream-check-v1).

The workflow scaffolds a throwaway R package from scratch with usethis::create_package() + usethis::use_cpp11(), attaches VTK by the two strategies described in the rvtk vignette, and asserts they produce byte-identical src/Makevars, src/Makevars.win, and tools/configure.R (the reference files are written to a neutral REF_DIR so every matrix leg compares against the same baseline). It then runs R CMD check on the scaffolded package.

The matrix

Twenty matrix legs (.github/workflows/downstream-check.yaml:55–103):

OS VTK strategy (× attach strategy)
macOS (release) system, prebuilt-static, built-shared (× manual / use_rvtk)
Windows (release) system, prebuilt-static, prebuilt-shared (× manual / use_rvtk)
Linux (release) system, prebuilt-static, built-shared (× manual / use_rvtk)
Linux (release) prebuilt-static-libcxx (× manual / use_rvtk)

The three VTK strategies mirror what a downstream package can encounter:

  • system — VTK installed from the OS package manager (Homebrew, apt, Rtools45 pacman), shared libraries.
  • prebuilt-static / prebuilt-shared — rvtk downloads its pre-built archives (static by default; VTK_LINK_TYPE=shared selects the Windows shared-DLL build).
  • built-shared — VTK configured from source with BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON and a curated 17-module list, installed into the runner (cached with cache-version: downstream-check-v1). This leg proves rvtk’s flags work against a shared VTK on the non-Windows platforms too.

The smoke test

The placeholder C++ file created by use_cpp11() is replaced by a small program (downstream-check.yaml:318–362) that deliberately spans several VTK modules so a single missing -l flag fails the link:

  • vtkPolyData — CommonDataModel
  • vtkPLYReader — IOPLY
  • vtkPNGReader — IOImage
  • vtkSphereSource — FiltersSources
  • vtkExtractGeometry — FiltersExtraction

(vtkCellGridReader / IOCellGrid is covered by the prebuilt-audit legs.)

The fedora-clang / libc++ legs

Two legs force the clang++ -stdlib=libc++ toolchain through R_MAKEVARS_USER, so rvtk’s configure detects libc++ and selects the *-linux-x86_64-libcxx archive. They then assert (downstream-check.yaml:252–278) that:

  • VTK_STDLIB in vtk.conf is exactly libc++; and
  • the downloaded libvtkscn archive is free of the libstdc++-ABI symbols (__try_use_facet, __cxa_call_terminate) that made 0.2.0 unloadable on CRAN’s r-devel-linux-x86_64-fedora-clang flavor (rvtk issue #15).

The checked-in comment at lines 78–84 of the workflow explains why this matters: CRAN compiles R packages with clang defaulting to libc++, which cannot dlopen a GCC/libstdc++-built archive.

The real consumer: riot-check.yaml

File: .github/workflows/riot-check.yaml (299 lines; workflow-level cache-version: riot-check-v1).

riot (tractoverse/riot) is the canonical real-world consumer of rvtk: its C++ reads and writes VTK bundle files (.vtk, .vtp). It was the package whose CI failures originally motivated rvtk’s pre-built archives, its module-linked flags, and the ABI guards, so it is the natural end-to-end test. Unlike downstream-check, this workflow does not scaffold a fake package: it checks out riot’s dev branch, installs it against the checked-out rvtk, and proves the link by processing riot’s real shipped files.

The matrix

Eleven legs (riot-check.yaml:63–75):

OS R VTK strategy
macOS (release) release system, prebuilt-static, built-shared
Windows (release) release system, prebuilt-static, prebuilt-shared
Linux devel prebuilt-static
Linux release system, prebuilt-static, built-shared
Linux oldrel-1 prebuilt-static

Version pinning

riot’s DESCRIPTION declares Imports: rvtk and Remotes: astamm/rvtk. To stop pak from silently pulling astamm/rvtk@main, the workflow installs the local checkout explicitly (riot-check.yaml:218–222):

pak::pkg_install(c("local::riot", "local::."), upgrade = FALSE, dependencies = TRUE)

and then asserts (riot-check.yaml:228–236) that the installed rvtk version equals the checked-out version, failing loudly if a silent downgrade would mask a regression.

The real file round-trip

The workflow reads riot’s legacy .vtk and XML .vtp bundles (UF_left.vtk / UF_left.vtp) with read_bundle(), writes one back with write_bundle(), and re-reads it (riot-check.yaml:244–261). This exercises exactly the VTK classes riot links against (vtkPolyDataReader, vtkXMLPolyDataReader, vtkPolyDataWriter, vtkXMLPolyDataWriter) — a stronger guarantee than a synthetic smoke test, and it exercises the writer path as well.

It then runs rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck() on riot (a clean source build through riot’s own Makevars → tools/configure.R → rvtk flag resolution) and riot’s tinytest suite.

CRAN checker environments: prebuilt-audit.yaml

File: .github/workflows/prebuilt-audit.yaml (244 lines).

Three of the eight archives — darwin-x86_64, linux-aarch64, and musl — cannot be exercised on hosted GitHub runners (build-vtk-libs.yml itself notes this for the musl job, which has to run docker run alpine:3.22 rather than a container: job because Actions’ Node.js runtime is glibc-linked). The prebuilt-audit workflow replicates the two CRAN checker environments that use those archives:

  1. Linux aarch64 (prebuilt-audit.yaml:36–131) — runs on ubuntu-24.04-arm inside ghcr.io/r-devel/rcheckserver/ubuntu:latest, the exact image CRAN’s linux-arm64 checker uses. It builds the rvtk source tarball, installs it, asserts the aarch64 archive was selected, runs the tinytest suite, then compiles, links, and runs a C++ program against the real archives (this is where vtkCellGridReader / IOCellGrid is baked into the smoke test).
  2. Linux x86_64 musl (prebuilt-audit.yaml:140–244) — runs inside ghcr.io/bastistician/rcheck-musl:latest (Alpine, R built against musl). Same recipe, asserting the musl archive is selected and that the busybox mktemp guard from 0.2.0’s fix still holds.

These legs exercise the configure-time download path (plain git fetch + R CMD build/INSTALL), which the other workflows only reach through pak::local_install().

How the archives themselves are validated

build-vtk-libs.yml (1177 lines) publishes the archives, but it also runs two quality gates on every build before packaging (plus the musl-specific guards):

  • Whole-archive link check (Linux job, build-vtk-libs.yml:641–672): an empty main linked with -Wl,--whole-archive over every static library, forcing every member object to resolve. This catches any internally inconsistent or dead module, including inter-module references that a consumer’s selective link would never pull in.
  • macOS deployment-target check (build-vtk-libs.yml:427–455 and 533–561): otool -l dumps LC_BUILD_VERSION for every member object of every static library and asserts minos == 13.0, the CMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET passed to configure. This is the regression guard for rvtk issue #16 (archives built on macOS 26 runners carried minos 26.0 and warned when linked into R packages targeting older macOS).
  • libc++-ABI check (libcxx job, build-vtk-libs.yml:844–885): the same __try_use_facet / __cxa_call_terminate scan that downstream-check re-runs on the downloaded archive, asserted before packaging (rvtk issue #15).
  • musl-specific guards: the Alpine build patches a viskores preprocessor test (build-vtk-libs.yml:945) and builds loguru with -DLOGURU_STACKTRACES=0 (build-vtk-libs.yml:986) because LOGURU_STACKTRACES on POSIX pulls in glibc-only backtrace symbols.

What is not covered by CI

  • The system-VTK behavior is only tested for the distributions the hosted runners provide (Homebrew on macOS, apt on Ubuntu, Rtools45 on Windows); CRAN’s own 13-flavor checks cover the rest.
  • Memory checkers: R CMD check’s Valgrind leg reports ~1.5 KB “definitely lost” inside VTK’s pipeline internals (vtkInformation, pipeline executives). This is inherent to the statically linked build and is suppressed with the shipped inst/valgrind/vtk.supp (see the “Memory checkers” section of the rvtk vignette); the pre-built distribution does not add a Valgrind clean-run gate.

Module-availability coverage

Every archive ships a vtk_modules.txt recording the exact module set it was built with, and available_modules() reports it at run time. The downstream-check smoke test links modules from five different kits (Common, IO, Filters, …) to prove the multi-module link works; the prebuilt-audit legs add a sixth (IOCellGrid). The full 160-library set (110 VTK kit modules, libvtksys, 23 viskores libraries, and 26 third-party libraries) is exercised as a whole* by the whole-archive link check at build time, and per-archive selection is asserted in both prebuilt-audit legs.

Summary

This is the integration-testing pyramid rvtk relies on:

  • many cheap assertions on a scaffolded consumer across every platform × VTK-strategy combination (downstream-check, 20 legs);
  • real-world proof on the package that motivated rvtk (riot-check, 11 legs);
  • environment-exact replication of the CRAN checkers no hosted runner can reach (prebuilt-audit, 2 legs); and
  • build-time gates that refuse to publish an archive that would fail any of the above (build-vtk-libs).

If you are writing a downstream package, the practical takeaway is: the strongest guarantee comes from the riot-check workflow — a real package with real VTK files. Add the same kind of round-trip test to your own package, and run it against both a system VTK and rvtk’s pre-built static archives.
